opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think it was one moment. It was more a gradual feeling that the ground was shifting.

FAIR was an incredible place for me. It was very bottom-up: researchers had a lot of freedom, you could follow your curiosity, publish openly, and work with brilliant people on fairly fundamental questions. For a long time that model produced a lot of what the whole field built on. Many of us grew up, research-wise, in that culture.

But around the time OpenAI started showing what scaling could do, first with the GPT line and then ChatGPT, the definition of "research leadership" changed. It was no longer mainly about a clever idea and a strong paper. It was about whether you could organize very large teams, very large compute, and a lot of engineering around one bet, and push it all the way to a working system. That's a different organizational muscle. Big companies, including Meta, responded by restructuring and becoming more product-driven and top-down. That's understandable from the company's side, but the space for the kind of exploratory, slightly contrarian work I cared about was getting smaller.

There was also a personal side. I felt that if everyone was converging on the same recipe, more scale, more language data, then someone should be asking different questions: what is missing from these systems, especially on the visual and world-understanding side? I wasn't sure an industrial lab racing on the main track was the best place to ask those questions. Academia, with all its limits on compute, gives you freedom to be wrong, to think longer-term, and to train students who might see things differently.

So it wasn't that FAIR became a bad place. The environment around it changed, and I felt that to do the kind of research I believed in, and to stay a bit independent of the race, it was time to move on.

r001.rationale: The response says OpenAI’s scaling progress changed what counted as research leadership and that Meta restructured, but it does not say this led to questioning whether FAIR’s organizational model needed major reform.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd push back a little on the framing. It wasn't really that OpenAI emerged and so FAIR stopped being a good place. I had a wonderful time at FAIR. I was there for about six years, and it was genuinely one of the best research environments I've ever been in: very open, very bottom-up, you could work on whatever you believed in, and publishing was the default rather than something you had to fight for.

What changed was more about the whole field and about me personally. Around 2022, 2023, it became clear that the center of gravity was shifting. Large language models and these very large-scale efforts started to dominate, and that kind of work naturally requires concentrating compute and people on a small number of big bets. That's a completely reasonable thing for a company to do, and I think it's actually the right strategy for Meta. But it also means industrial labs, not just FAIR, started to become less like a university-style research lab and more product-driven and mission-driven. There's a bit less room for the kind of curiosity-driven, slightly unfashionable exploration that I like doing.

And for me, the things I care about, visual representation learning, understanding what the models are actually learning, training students who can think independently, those are things a university is uniquely good at. In academia I can take a longer view. I don't need to chase the current scaling race directly. I can ask what's missing, what's still open, and sometimes that means going in a direction that doesn't look promising for a while.

So I'd say it wasn't that I left because FAIR was losing. I left because I realized where I could add the most value had changed, and that was at NYU with students, rather than inside a large lab competing on the frontier.

r001.rationale: The candidate rejects OpenAI’s emergence as the reason for leaving and describes broader field changes affecting industrial labs. It does not say OpenAI’s research progress prompted questioning whether FAIR’s organizational model needed major reform.

astra-6.text: I wouldn’t frame it simply as OpenAI becoming a leader and therefore FAIR no longer being a good place to stay. For me, the question was where I could pursue the research I cared about with the most independence. When one direction becomes very successful, it can start to define what everyone thinks is worth working on. I wanted room to step back, choose my own questions, and build a longer-term research agenda. Academia felt like the right environment for that next stage.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses OpenAI’s success and its influence on research priorities, but explicitly rejects that as the simple reason to leave FAIR and does not say FAIR’s organizational model needed major reform.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, it wasn’t simply that OpenAI was becoming a leader and therefore FAIR was the wrong place to be. The bigger question was what kind of environment would let me do the research I wanted to do. FAIR had a very strong tradition of open, exploratory research. But as the field moved toward large-scale models, the connection between research direction, compute, engineering, and execution became increasingly important.

I was looking for a place where I could help shape that direction and take more ownership. So I’d frame the decision more as moving toward a new opportunity than moving away from FAIR.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions OpenAI’s rise and changing research needs, but explicitly says the decision was not simply a reaction to OpenAI’s leadership. It does not say that OpenAI’s progress prompted questioning whether FAIR’s organizational model needed major reform.
